name: Real-website re-run of the busy-CPU leak (plan v2, Phase 1b)
code: main at 4466516 (wire clock with the relay's fixed window), tools/wf_real.py
setup: 20 real sites x 2 loads per round x 5 interleaved rounds per variant; headless Firefox and the client data plane on cores 0,1, relay/exit/capture on 2,3; capture on the client link (an ISP's view); fixed 12 s window; on mains; k-FP closed world, 5-fold, via tools/wf_deep.py (the pipeline that reproduces the pilot's 99.16% and 81.31% exactly).

variants.clock: fast + wire clock 4,000 pps, catch-up 50 ms, fq on the client link

findings: The wire clock cuts k-FP from 34.4% (fast) to 9.5% (chance 5%) on real websites with the browser sharing the data plane's cores.
The busy-CPU leak is in the upstream: fast scores 37.0% on upstream packets alone and 9.0% on downstream alone; the clock brings upstream to 9.0%.

A small residual remains: 9.5% beats all 20 shuffled-label runs (mean 4.45%, max 8.42%; p = 0.048, the resolution of 20 permutations). It is about the same in both directions (9.0% up, 10.5% down) and the downstream part matches fast's own downstream (9.0%): the relay's downstream is not clocked.

fast scored 34.4% here, not the pilot's 81%: the busy-CPU leak's size depends on the setup (here 1 worker, 2 loads per site per round, 5 rounds interleaved). The control is still strongly above chance.
Cost: the clock's 30 ms look-ahead adds about 28 ms to the upstream round trip; heavy pages time out more often (clock 180 of 200 loads ok, fast 192, undefended 194).
Every clock pass kept its tunnel up (the relay fix): before it, round-1 and round-2 clock passes had 1 and 0 of 40 loads.
next: Re-run with the relay's clock on (both directions clocked), on mains power and an otherwise idle machine.
More permutations (100+) and more sites/loads for a tighter residual estimate.
A shorter look-ahead, measured for its busy-CPU cost.
status: Strong evidence for the wire clock, not yet a default: residual downstream leak, a latency cost, and one 20-site closed-world setup.

residual_by_direction_100_permutations.method: k-FP on the clock run, each direction alone and both, against 100 shuffled-label runs each (tools/wf_residual.py; rerun-20261115b/RESIDUAL_clock.json)
residual_by_direction_100_permutations.downstream_top_features: inter-arrival gaps: all-packet 75th percentile and maximum, downstream 75th percentile, maximum and spread
residual_by_direction_100_permutations.reading: In this run the residual was in the downstream (p = 0.0099) and not the upstream (p = 0.079). It did not replicate: in re-run 2 the client-only clock's residual sat in the upstream (p = 0.040) and not the downstream (p = 0.49), so the residual's direction is not stable across runs (docs/evidence/WF_REAL_RERUN2.json). Clocking both directions brought the full attack to chance there (5.15%, p = 0.58).
